tower-dq18x2.name: Tower
tower-dq18x2.summary: An air traffic controller for your deadlines. Tower reads the rulebook, watches your work unattended for weeks, and calls your phone before you lose on a technicality.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They built the thing that survives the no-budget, no-internet, no-permission case.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: An air traffic controller for your deadlines. Tower reads the rulebook, watches your work unattended for weeks, and calls your phone before you lose on a technicality.
steal_this: Replace chat turns with a scheduled process that wakes on a condition. Patience is a feature nobody else ships.
Anything the architecture can enforce, the architecture enforces. Probabilistic components get proposals; deterministic components get verdicts.
Classify each step as judgement vs. format vs. volume, then route. Save the frontier model for the one call everything downstream depends on.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then Tower made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any agent that touches production data

audit.worth_note: The stealable part is not hackathon-rule-watching, it is the outcome model: three terminal states in which UNVERIFIED is neither satisfied nor unmet, an agent that retracts its own finding when the evidence turns out to have been there all along, and a coverage line reported out loud ('five of ten applicable, here are the five I could not check'). Every verification record in this corpus - ComplianceGuardian, VMS AI Guard, Continuity - has the monitoring loop and none of them has retraction, and the author's eighth defect (a 200 that was really a login wall, with the harness green the whole time it existed) is the argument for why a boolean is the wrong return type for a checker. Held back from 'breakthrough' on evidence, not on idea: there is no repository, no live deployment we can reach, one like, and the only number a reader can verify independently is the F1 arithmetic - recall reconciles exactly against the published 29-obligation key, precision's denominator never appears. The pattern is worth taking today; the build cannot be inspected.

artifact_exists.why: no source repo linked, but the page publishes a working artifact: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gDaQpZghCN0

build_is_real.why: no repository published, so the build cannot be read

limits_disclosed.why: the team stated where the system fails, in production terms (fail)

numbers_add_up.why: 1 figure(s) we re-derived do not match the page (1 did reconcile): a thirty-minute schedule without the idempotency guard 'phones you ninety six times a day about the same missing file' — contradicted by the page's own stated cadence: every thirty minutes is 48 ticks a day, not 96; 96 is what a fifteen-minute schedule would give. The guard's necessity is unaffected - one call per tick per open finding is still dozens a day - but this is the one figure on the page that its own inputs refute, and it is quoted here rather than smoothed over

stack_consistency.why: no repo to cross-check the declared stack against

test_or_eval_evidence.why: a measured evaluation with a stated denominator is described on the page (an A/B comparison or a logged-outcome harness counts; a bare 'we tested it' does not)

assumptions: a rulebook per competition small enough to enumerate as obligations - the eval key here is 29 items, and a hundred-page rulebook with nested exceptions changes the extraction problem, not just the prompt

reachable artifacts with stable identities: the whole design depends on mapping a requirement to a URL, file or video that can be re-fetched anonymously, so a private repo or an unlisted video is a checker you cannot write
a telephony channel with call-status callbacks if you want retraction to mean anything (Twilio-shaped, and it needs an opt-in consent path for the number)
somebody to read the UNVERIFIED list - the honest output of this design is a report that says 'I could not check these five', which is only an asset in an org that will act on it
clone_cost.estimate: 3-4 weeks for the four-agent skeleton on one rulebook; add a week per artifact class you want checked honestly, and a day or two per new competition to hand-write the ground truth
clone_cost.why: The control flow is the cheap part and the page says so: two model calls total, a pure function for the state machine, a policy table for escalation, FastAPI on Cloud Run with Firestore state and a scheduler - an engineer who has shipped a cron with a queue can build that in a week or two. The cost is everywhere else. Each requirement class needs a real checker against a real surface (GitHub contents API, HEAD requests that can distinguish a login wall from a page, YouTube oEmbed, the platform's own project page), each with its own auth and 200-lies-to-you edge cases; the phone path needs idempotency, call-history and stand-down semantics; the extraction needs a hand-written obligation key per rulebook before you can say anything at all about whether it worked; and 'unknown' has to be threaded through the data model from the start, which is a refactor in any codebase where a boolean is already doing the work. The escalation number they quote as the reason (48 evaluations a day, not the 96 the page says) is exactly the kind of detail that has to be re-derived per deployment rather than copied.

audit.what_to_steal: Make 'could not check' a value that propagates, not a gap that defaults to a verdict: UNVERIFIED is distinct from UNMET, blank config is distinct from failure, and an unknown premise in a conditional defaults to false rather than being narrated into existence. Then steal the two honesty mechanics that fall out of it - retraction as a first-class action (call back and stand down your own alert, and if you were wrong say RETRACTED, with call history as an input to narration so you cannot apologise for a call you never made), and routing by extracted content instead of model-generated identifiers, because slugs change between extraction runs and content does not.
audit.what_breaks_first: The requirement-to-tool-surface mapping. Every requirement needs a real place to look, and the failure mode the author hit first is a silent one: 9 of 12 requirements lost their route and reported as unverifiable. Anything the agent cannot reach - a private repo, an unlisted video, a platform page behind a login wall, a URL that returns 200 on a sign-in form - becomes a permanent UNVERIFIED, which is the correct answer and the one that makes the product look useless to a user who wants a green tick. Second is the severity policy: 'Kill calls immediately, Major waits until seven days out, Minor never calls' is tuned to one rulebook's shape, and a second competition with different disqualification clauses needs the table re-cut, not re-used. Third is the measured weakness they name themselves - extraction is structurally biased toward 'what must the entrant DO' over standing eligibility and legal clauses, and dedup folds adjacent legal text away - so the requirements most likely to cost you the prize are the ones the classifier is worst at.

prior_art.relation: shares the load-bearing trick - every verdict carries the words of the rule it came from - but the surfaces are opposite: ComplianceGuardian scores an uploaded document and auto-approves routine cases, Tower watches live artifacts on a schedule and refuses to approve anything it cannot reach

closest structural sibling in the corpus: scheduled, unattended monitoring of live state against a named rulebook with escalation to a human. VMS AI Guard is held to the pool as thin for lack of any evaluation; Tower is the same shape with the evidence VMS lacks - a hand-written ground-truth key and a published precision/recall trajectory

both exist because truth decays without anyone editing it, and both answer by re-checking against a live source and drafting the fix for a human; Continuity's unit is a wiki fact, Tower's is an obligation, and Continuity has no equivalent of Tower's retraction path

same trust budget from the other side: Kora buys its autonomy by shrinking human attention to '10 minutes of approvals a week', Tower buys it by making the agent's own uncertainty and reversals part of what the human sees

adversarial-compliance-matrix.summary: Gemini-Box: Immutable cryptographic claims for Gemini agents. Any bit flip -> instant INVALID.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They built the thing that survives the no-budget, no-internet, no-permission case.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: Gemini-Box: Immutable cryptographic claims for Gemini agents. Any bit flip -> instant INVALID.
steal_this: Adopt one boring enterprise discipline (append-only audit, signed config, replay on boot) and let it be the reason a buyer trusts you.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then Gemini-Box made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any tool with an expensive generation step

audit.worth_note: The part worth keeping is the smallest credible security demo there is: a fixture generator plus a fixed scenario matrix wired into CI, so the artifact is a run rather than a slide. It is merged into the sibling submission because both pages describe one platform by one author, and the split version publishes twice the entries for half the evidence.

artifact_exists.why: no source repo linked, but the page publishes a working artifact: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Uix0Pzf8YqY

build_is_real.why: no repository published, so the build cannot be read

limits_disclosed.why: the team described how hard the build was, but not a limitation of the system itself — no accuracy, coverage, privacy or failure-mode statement

numbers_add_up.why: 1 figure(s) a reader can check against the product (twelve attack scenarios in the simulation matrix), but 1 headline figure(s) carry no testable denominator: 100% successful compilation and green test run on the first attempt

stack_consistency.why: no repo to cross-check the declared stack against

test_or_eval_evidence.why: a harness is described (ci, fixture) but no result, run link or case count is published, so it cannot be checked

assumptions: you use a published attack corpus rather than only your own fixtures
you link the repo and the CI run, or the number is decoration
clone_cost.estimate: 2 days for a Rust validator with a fixture generator and a CI matrix
clone_cost.why: the engine is small and the harness is standard cargo plus actions; the expensive part is sourcing real payloads, which this project did not do

audit.what_to_steal: gen_fixtures.rs as a test *generator*: emit the clean and adversarial cases from the same spec the validator consumes, then let CI rebuild the whole matrix on every commit. It makes a regression impossible to hide and costs one file.
audit.what_breaks_first: A suite whose cases and fixtures are both authored by the system measures agreement with itself, so '12 of 12' says nothing about the attack space it did not write; and the pass claim is not reachable at all here - no repository, workflow URL or run id is linked. The honest next step for a clone is an external corpus of real malicious samples with a published miss rate.

prior_art.relation: same author's same platform - this page is one component of it, which is why the records are merged
runtime guardrails plus auditability for agents, delivered as middleware instead of a validator
compliance fleet that leans on vendor guardrails - same 'policy as code' instinct, less proof
